erros.devolutiva: Relembrar que o numerador representa a quantidade total de itens e o denominador representa o tamanho do grupo.
Reforçar que converter para número misto apenas muda a forma de escrita, não o tamanho da unidade fracionária.

dicas.texto: Você está indo muito bem! Pense: quantas vezes o número 4 cabe inteiramente dentro do 9? Esse será o seu número inteiro.
Tente dividir 9 por 4. O quociente vai no campo da parte inteira (m1) e o resto da divisão será o novo numerador (m2).
O denominador (m3) continua sendo o mesmo da fração original. Quantas vezes 4 cabe em 9 e quanto sobra?
Você quase lá! 4 vezes 2 é 8. Para chegar em 9, falta apenas 1. Então, coloque 2 no campo m1, 1 no campo m2 e mantenha o 4 no campo m3.
Lembre-se que a reta está dividida em 4 partes iguais entre cada número inteiro. Onde ficaria a primeira marca depois do 2?
Localize o número 2 na reta. Como a fração é 1/4, você deve avançar apenas uma das quatro divisões após o 2.
Conte uma marca após o número 2. Cada marca representa 1/4.
Coloque o ponto exatamente na primeira marcação logo à direita do número 2.

interfaceCtat.descricao: Interface FIXA do tutor (a mesma tela para todos os problemas): enunciado; pergunta "What is the fraction in the problem? Convert it to mixed fraction form if it will help you." com duas caixas numéricas (f1 em cima = numerador, f2 embaixo = denominador); botão "Convert" que abre as caixas do número misto (m1 = parte inteira, m2/m3 = fração restante; "-" quando não há); reta numérica de 0 a 3 (numline) onde o aluno marca um ponto, com encaixe em 4 partes por unidade (marcas ocultas); texto de apoio na reta: "The number hint is off in this problem!"; botão Hint; botão Done. Os passos do aluno são ações NESSES componentes (digitar nos campos, converter, marcar o ponto, concluir).

erros.devolutiva: The numerator represents the total number of smaller bottles, while the denominator represents how many smaller bottles fill one larger bottle. Keep the total in the numerator.
The fractional part is still measured in fourths. Converting to a mixed number changes the form, but the denominator remains 4.
The denominator describes the size of each group, so it remains the original denominator 4 rather than becoming the total 9.

erros.devolutiva: Only two complete groups of four fit into nine. The leftover amount must be represented as a fractional part rather than rounding up.

dicas.texto: Look for the number that represents the total amount of water bottles John has.
Place the total number of smaller bottles in the top box of the fraction.
The top box should contain the number of bottles being shared among the larger bottles.
Read the total number of smaller bottles in the problem and type that number into f1.
Focus on the size of each group of smaller bottles.
Place the number of smaller bottles needed for one larger bottle in the bottom box.
The denominator describes the number of smaller bottles held by each larger bottle.
Read how many smaller bottles fit into one larger bottle and type that number into f2.
Compare the numerator and denominator to decide whether the fraction is greater than one.
When the numerator is larger, use the conversion control to show whole groups and a remaining fraction.
The fraction represents more than one complete larger bottle, so the mixed-number fields must be opened.
Click the button labeled ... to open the fields for the whole part and the remaining fraction.
Think about how many complete groups the denominator makes and what remains afterward.
Divide the numerator by the denominator; use the quotient for the whole part and the remainder for the new numerator.
The denominator fits into the numerator twice, leaves one item, and the denominator remains unchanged.
Enter the quotient in m1, the remainder in m2, and keep the original denominator in m3.
Use the whole-number part first, then locate the fractional part between two consecutive integers.
Find 2 on the number line and divide the interval from 2 to 3 into four equal parts.
The point belongs between 2 and 3, one equal quarter-step after 2.
Place the point at the first quarter mark to the right of 2, then submit that marked position.
Before finishing, check that the point represents the mixed number from the conversion.
Review the point's position relative to 2 and 3 and confirm that it is on a quarter mark.
The point should be between 2 and 3, at the first subdivision after 2.
When the point is in the correct quarter position, click the button labeled ....

exercicio.statement:
John has 9 bottles of water, and wishes to move them to bigger water bottles. Each larger water bottle can hold water from 4 smaller bottles. If he moves water from all of the smaller water bottles, how many of the larger water bottles would be filled? Show the amount on the number line.
What is the fraction in the problem? Convert it to mixed fraction form if it will help you.
